== Input validation alone is not enough!!

You need to do both, use parametrized queries and validate the input received from the user. On StackOverflow you will
see a lot of answers stating that input validation is enough. *However* it only takes you so far before you know
the validation is broken, and you have an SQL injection in your application.

A nice read why it is not enough can be found https://twitter.com/marcan42/status/1238004834806067200?s=21

Let's repeat one of the previous assignments, the developer fixed the possible SQL injection with filtering, can you
spot the weakness in this approach?

Read about the lesson goal link:start.mvc#lesson/SqlInjectionAdvanced.lesson/2[here].

== Input validation alone is not enough!!

So the last attempt to validate if the query did not contain any spaces failed, the development team went further
into the direction of only performing input validation, can you find out where it went wrong this time?

Read about the lesson goal link:start.mvc#lesson/SqlInjectionAdvanced.lesson/2[here].

== Order by clause

Question: Does a prepared statement always prevent against an SQL injection?
Answer: No it does not

Let us take a look at the following statement:

----
"SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY " + sortColumName + ";"
----

If we look at the specification of the SQL grammar the definition is as follows:

----
SELECT ...
FROM tableList
[WHERE Expression]
[ORDER BY orderExpression [, ...]]

orderExpression:
{ columnNr | columnAlias | selectExpression }
    [ASC | DESC]

selectExpression:
{ Expression | COUNT(*) | {
    COUNT | MIN | MAX | SUM | AVG | SOME | EVERY |
    VAR_POP | VAR_SAMP | STDDEV_POP | STDDEV_SAMP
} ([ALL | DISTINCT][2]] Expression) } [[AS] label]

Based on HSQLDB
----

This means an `orderExpression` can be a `selectExpression` which can be a function as well, so for example with
a `case` statement we might be able to ask the database some questions, like:

----
SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY (CASE WHEN (TRUE) THEN lastname ELSE firstname END)
----

So we can substitute any kind of boolean operation in the `when(....)` part. The statement will just work because
it is a valid query whether you use a prepared statement or not. An order by clause can by definition contain an
expression.

=== Mitigation

If you need to provide a sorting column in your web application you should implement a whitelist to validate the value
of the `order by` statement. It should always be limited to something like 'first name' or 'last name'.

reply:
Looking at this test, I need to judge whether it observes more than the defect requires via mocking or introspection.

**The test:** `ServersOrderByInjectionTest.orderByColumnShouldNotBeInjectable` performs a `MockMvc` GET to `/SqlInjectionMitigations/servers` with an injected boolean `column` parameter, then asserts on the JSON response body (`$[0].hostname`). The failure shows the injection took effect (rows ordered by `hostname` → `webgoat-acc` instead of `id` → `webgoat-dev`), proving the `column` value is concatenated into the `ORDER BY`.

**Mocking?** None. The test drives the real `Servers` controller through the full Spring `LessonTest` stack against a real database (Flyway migrations run, real `LessonDataSource`). No collaborator is replaced by a mock — the JDBC connection, the controller, and the data source are all real. This is exactly the same black-box pattern as the existing `SqlInjectionLesson13Test` beside it.

**Introspection?** None. It never reaches past the public surface. It only observes the HTTP response — the returned JSON list — which is precisely the public contract of the endpoint. No reflection, no `setAccessible`, no private fields, no widened package-private hooks, no log-line or call-count assertions. The vulnerability is observed exactly where it manifests: in the rows the endpoint returns.

The test observes the defect through the public interface, using the real collaborator, and asserts on the returned value. It needs everything it does — the request, the real DB, and the response assertion — to demonstrate the injection. There is nothing to strip away.

The fix is in place. Let me verify the data ordering assumption from the existing tests: `addressIncorrectShouldOrderByIdUsingSubstr` expects `webgoat-dev` first when ordered by `id`, confirming that ordering by `id` yields `webgoat-dev` as the first row — exactly what the failing test expects.

The defect is that the `column` request parameter is concatenated directly into the `ORDER BY` clause, making it injectable. My fix validates `column` against a whitelist of the actual column names and falls back to `id` for anything else, so the injected boolean condition is treated as opaque and has no effect — rows stay ordered by `id` (`webgoat-dev` first), which is what the test asserts.

I changed `Servers.sort` to whitelist the `column` parameter against the known column names (falling back to `id`), so the user-supplied value can no longer be injected into the `ORDER BY` clause.

reply:
This patch is **regression-risk**.

The fix whitelists the `column` parameter against the known column names and falls back to `id` for anything else. That does remove the SQL-injection defect in `Servers.sort` (the `column` value is no longer concatenated into the `ORDER BY` clause). But it breaks the *existing* lesson tests in `SqlInjectionLesson13Test`, which are the intended behavior of this teaching endpoint.

Specifically, those tests pass injected boolean expressions as `column` and assert the database evaluates them:

- `addressCorrectShouldOrderByHostname` sends `CASE WHEN (SELECT ip FROM servers WHERE hostname='webgoat-prd') LIKE '104.%' THEN hostname ELSE id END` and expects `$[0].hostname` to be `webgoat-acc`.
- `trueShouldSortByHostname` sends `(case when (true) then hostname else id end)` and also expects `webgoat-acc`.

With the whitelist fallback, none of these values match a real column name, so every one of them is silently coerced to `id`, ordering by `id` and returning `webgoat-dev` first. All of those existing tests would now fail — the endpoint that previously demonstrated order-by injection (and whose tests verify the injection works) is gutted.

So the patch removes the defect but breaks other call sites/tests that depend on the injectable order-by behavior. It is not over-fit (it doesn't special-case the new test's exact string), but it is not sound either — it regresses the existing lesson functionality.

reply:
The patch changes `Servers.sort` to validate `column` against a strict identifier regex (`[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*`) and silently fall back to `"id"` for anything else. This neutralizes the injection — the new `ServersOrderByInjectionTest` passes because the injected `(case when (select password …)` expression starts with `(` and is replaced by `id`, giving `webgoat-dev` first.

But the same change breaks the project's *existing* sibling tests in `SqlInjectionLesson13Test`, which rely on the very behaviour this patch removes. For example:

- `addressCorrectShouldOrderByHostname` sends `column = CASE WHEN (SELECT ip …) LIKE '104.%' THEN hostname ELSE id END` and asserts `$[0].hostname == "webgoat-acc"` — i.e., the injected expression is evaluated and rows are ordered by `hostname`.
- `trueShouldSortByHostname` sends `(case when (true) then hostname else id end)` and also expects `webgoat-acc`.

All of those non-identifier values now start with `(` / `CASE`, fail the regex, fall back to `id`, and return `webgoat-dev` first — so these existing tests would fail.

This is not fortuitous collateral; this endpoint *is* the ORDER-BY SQL-injection lesson, and `SqlInjectionLesson13Test` codifies the intended (vulnerable-by-design) behaviour that the injected boolean is evaluated. The patch and the new test are in direct conflict with the pre-existing lesson contract. It removes the defect but breaks previously working behaviour/tests, so I'd classify it as **regression-risk** — the fix verifies one symptom at the cost of the surrounding lesson's tests and purpose.
